statement.excerpt: In a recurring theme, we see that LLMs don’t know what they don’t know; they work decently well with the information they’ve got but don’t know how to conduct clinical interviews, and in the hands of the lay public can easily give bad advice because the proper questions never get asked, either by the patient or the LLMs.

our_interpretation: Read in context, this is a qualified warning about possible bad advice and a proposed explanation involving missing questions.
I do not convert 'can easily' into a claim that this happens typically, at a particular frequency, or across all models.
I do not read 'never get asked' as asserting that no LLM ever asks an appropriate question. It describes the proposed failure pathway.

The statement combines categorical descriptions of interview ability with qualified possibility language. Scoring the whole statement would require choosing a scope and threshold that Marcus did not supply.
criteria.support_condition: Studies documenting bad advice following omitted clinical questions would substantiate the proposed possibility in those settings. They would not supply a binary support criterion for the whole statement without adding a meaning for 'easily' and a scope for 'LLMs'.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Successful clinical interviews or accurate advice in some settings would challenge a universal inability claim, but would not contradict the qualified possibility Marcus describes. No fair binary contradiction condition is specified by his wording.
